title: Explain common OS types and their purposes

subtopics.heading: macOS file types and application management
subtopics.notes:
Key file extensions:
- .dmg - Apple Disk Image. Mounts as a virtual drive in Finder. macOS equivalent of an ISO.
- .pkg - Installer package. Runs a script-based installer. macOS equivalent of setup.exe.
- .app - Application bundle. Not a single executable - it is a folder containing all the app's files. Double-click to launch. Right-click > View Package Contents to see inside.

Uninstalling apps:
- Most apps: drag the .app to Trash. Deleting the bundle removes everything.
- Some apps include a formal Uninstaller.app - run it instead.
- No Programs and Features equivalent; use Finder > Applications.

App Store - centralized repository. Manages updates automatically or manually. Click user name at bottom-left for full install history.
subtopics.whyOnExam: .dmg is disk image, .pkg is installer, .app is the application bundle. Uninstall = delete the .app. No setup.exe on macOS.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming macOS has no uninstaller. Most apps just need the .app deleted, but some DO include an uninstaller.

subtopics.heading: macOS special folders
subtopics.notes:
/Applications - all installed apps. Equivalent to Windows Program Files.
/Users - one sub-folder per user account. Equivalent to Windows Users.
/Library - shared support files (scripts, fonts) used by multiple apps and users.
~/Library - per-user library (~ = home directory). Hidden by default in Finder. Path example: /Users/professor/Library.
/System - macOS operating system files. Equivalent to Windows\System32 area.

All paths use forward slash. The home directory is /Users/<username>, denoted as ~ in the shell.
subtopics.whyOnExam: ~ means the current user's home directory. /Library vs ~/Library is a common distinction.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing /Library (system-wide) with ~/Library (per-user). The per-user folder is hidden by default.

subtopics.heading: Apple ID, Managed Apple ID, and MDM
subtopics.notes:
Apple ID - personal identifier tied to App Store, iCloud, device ownership.

Managed Apple ID
- Business/education version managed by IT via Apple Business Manager.
- Can integrate with Active Directory - same credentials as Windows login.
- Works with MDM (Mobile Device Manager) for central device management.
- IT can push apps, assign permissions, control data access across all devices.

Time Machine (backup)
- Built-in backup application. Backs up to an external or network volume.
- Hourly backups for the past 24 hours.
- Daily backups for the past month.
- Weekly backups for all previous months.
- When volume fills up, oldest backups are deleted automatically.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Time Machine backup schedule: hourly/daily/weekly. Managed Apple ID = corporate context, integrates with AD.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing Time Machine (local/network backup) with iCloud (cloud sync). They are separate features.

subtopics.heading: macOS software updates and Rapid Security Response
subtopics.notes:
OS updates: System Settings > General > Software Updates.
App updates: App Store (separate from OS updates).

Update options:
- Download updates automatically
- Install macOS updates (can be turned off)
- Install App Store app updates automatically
- Install security responses and system files
- Beta updates (off by default - unstable)

Rapid Security Response (RSR)
- Emergency security patches pushed immediately for critical vulnerabilities.
- Available on macOS, iOS, and iPadOS.
- Turned on by default under Automatic Updates.
- If an OS version has a letter suffix (e.g., 14.1.1a), an RSR update has been applied.
subtopics.whyOnExam: RSR = emergency critical patch, pushed immediately. Letter appended to version number after RSR.
subtopics.commonTrap: Treating RSR as optional. It is on by default and addresses critical vulnerabilities, not routine updates.

subtopics.heading: macOS System Preferences (System Settings)
subtopics.notes:
macOS equivalent of the Windows Control Panel. Single location for all OS settings.

Key sections:
- Display - arrange monitors, set resolution, brightness, color profiles, menu bar location.
- Network - configure wired/wireless adapters, IPv4/IPv6, DHCP or static, DNS, 802.1X auth, proxy, hardware settings.
- Printers and Scanners - add printers, share them on the network, view queues, check ink/toner.
- Privacy and Security - per-app permissions (location, microphone, camera, photos, files/folders). FileVault toggle.
- Accessibility - vision, hearing, and input accommodations. Third-party accessibility apps need explicit permission here.
- Time Machine - configure backup volumes (direct or network).

In newer macOS versions, called System Settings rather than System Preferences.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Firewall and FileVault are found under Privacy and Security. Network adapter properties mirror Windows adapter settings.
subtopics.commonTrap: Looking for antivirus in System Preferences. macOS has no built-in single AV app - third-party only.

subtopics.heading: macOS key features
subtopics.notes:
Finder - file management front end. Equivalent to Windows File Explorer. Provides access to local drives, network shares, and screen sharing targets.

Spotlight - system-wide search. Launch with Command+Space. Searches apps, documents, images, websites, and more. Customize categories in System Preferences > Spotlight.

Mission Control - shows all running apps spread across the desktop. Activate: 3-finger swipe up OR Control+Up arrow.
- Spaces: multiple virtual desktops, managed from within Mission Control.

Keychain - encrypted credential store built into macOS. Stores passwords, certificates, secure notes. Decrypted with the user's login password. Not an add-on - built-in.

iCloud - cloud sync across Apple devices. Syncs calendar, email, photos, messages. iCloud Drive = file cloud storage (like Dropbox).

Continuity - seamless handoff between macOS, iPadOS, iOS devices. Pick up a task started on one device on another. Also: iPhone as Mac webcam, AirDrop file transfer, text message forwarding. Requires iCloud login on all devices.

Disk Utility - graphical tool to manage file systems. Format drives, create partitions, mount/unmount volumes, create disk images.

FileVault - full disk encryption. macOS equivalent of BitLocker. Uses login password or iCloud credentials to encrypt the entire drive. Enable/disable: System Preferences > Privacy and Security > FileVault.

Terminal - command-line interface app. Used to run shell scripts and manage the OS.

Force Quit - terminate a hung application.
- Keyboard: Command+Option+Escape (shows Force Quit window).
- Dock: hold Option, right-click the app icon > Force Quit.
subtopics.whyOnExam: FileVault = macOS full disk encryption (BitLocker equivalent). Spotlight = Command+Space. Force Quit = Command+Option+Escape. Keychain = encrypted credentials store.
subtopics.commonTrap: Calling Spaces a separate macOS feature. Spaces ARE Mission Control - they are managed from within the Mission Control interface, not separately.
